title: Seller-Brain Capture and Margin Leak Audit
one_liner: In the 90-day handover, reverse-engineer the retiring owner's pricing and rules of thumb from years of quotes and invoices, and find the contract and price leaks the seller never fixed, for a fee tied to recovered margin.
customer: First-time acquirers (search funders, independent sponsors, SBA-financed buyers, small holdcos) of $1-15M revenue service and light-manufacturing firms. SBA lenders and brokers are secondary referrers.
problem: The seller's pricing logic lives in his head, records are paper or Excel, and the handover is a 'handshake and good luck'. New owners find contractual minimums unbilled, price books frozen for years, parts sold below cost, and waste in telecom and software. They discover this only after closing, when the seller is already leaving.
solution: A 30-day sprint at signing or close. (1) Ingest 3 years of quotes, invoices, price books, contracts and vendor, phone and SaaS bills, including scanned paper. (2) An AI model reconstructs the implicit pricing rules and flags exceptions. (3) A structured, recorded 3-hour seller interview validates and labels the rules. (4) Output a working quote calculator, a written 'rules of thumb' manual, and a ranked leak list in dollars (unbilled contractual minimums, stale prices vs inflation, below-cost jobs and parts, dead subscriptions). The seller reviews the model weekly during the transition period.
why_now: Bain's 2026 reports say deals now need 10-12% EBITDA growth to hit returns and 79% of GPs expect flat purchase multiples, so operational upside has to be found rather than bought. Buyers of small firms feel the same pressure. LLMs now read messy PDFs, scans and Excel cheaply, which makes a 10-day audit cost a few hundred dollars in compute instead of a consultant's month.
revenue_model: $4-6K fixed fee for the capture sprint, plus 10-15% of annualized recovered margin in year one (capped). Optional pre-LOI 'upside memo' at $1.5-2.5K that buyers use to justify a bid and negotiate price.
non_obvious_insight: The leaks are contractual and forgotten, not strategic, and the seller's pricing logic is a perishable asset that expires with the transition period. Concrete cases from ETA operators: Tew & Taylor's contracts specified a two-hour minimum but the prior owner billed one hour, and after the buyer applied the contract rate there was 'virtually no customer pushback' (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). At Cardinal Heating & Air, prices were unchanged since pre-COVID, parts were sold below cost, and the buyer cut $1.4M of annualized cost in two weeks ($10K/month in cell phones vs $3K needed). Gross margins went from 7-20% to 48-49% (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/mike-bourgeois-cardinal-heating-and-air). At Winsor Fireform, pricing was the seller's 27 years of 'hunches', and the buyers 'sprinted' to extract it into a model during his 3-month transition; gross margin rose from 55% to 58-59% (https://acquiringminds.co/articles/andrew-sova-alex-clark-winsor-fireform-novo-foundry). At Gary Air, prices had not kept pace with inflation for 4+ years, and earnings went from $340K SDE to $1.3M EBITDA in 14 months (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/rob-brooks-gary-air). Four independent buyers found the same class of leak and each rebuilt it by hand.
first_30_days: Offer free audits to 10 first-time buyers found in ETA communities (Searchfunder, Acquiring Minds audience, ETA subreddits) in exchange for permission to publish anonymized before/after numbers. Build parsers for QuickBooks exports and for invoice exports from ServiceTitan, Jobber and Housecall Pro, plus a vendor-bill classifier. Create a one-page seller-interview protocol. Convert the first 3 free audits into case studies, then switch to contingency pricing.

title: Dry-Hole Atlas for Hydrogen, Helium, Geothermal
one_liner: Re-read a century of scanned well logs and gas analyses, once treated as junk, to find natural hydrogen, helium and hot rock, and sell the resulting atlas to exploration companies by area of interest.
customer: Junior exploration companies and VC-backed developers in natural hydrogen, helium and geothermal (and lithium-brine plays), plus land and mineral-lease advisors who need leads. They pay for subscriptions and area-of-interest data packs.
problem: The US has millions of drilled wells. Old records include gas analyses, bottom-hole temperatures, water chemistry and mud-log shows, mostly recorded as incidental noise by oil and gas operators. They sit as scanned TIFFs and PDFs at state geological surveys and core repositories. New subsurface commodities need exactly this once-discarded information. Oil-and-gas data vendors index hydrocarbon fields, not hydrogen, helium or heat, and small explorers cannot afford to hire teams to dig through archives across 30 state surveys.
solution: A scan-to-structured-data pipeline across public state survey archives. Extract gas composition (hydrogen, helium, nitrogen), bottom-hole temperature and depth, and brine chemistry. Geolocate every record, correct for known temperature-log biases, and publish a queryable map atlas with prospectivity layers per township or section. Sell by area of interest. Offer custom queries such as 'every well within 20 miles of this substation with more than 0.3% helium and temperature above 150 C at 3 km'.
why_now: AI data centers are driving huge demand for clean firm power, and geothermal developers are raising large rounds and signing hyperscaler offtakes. Natural hydrogen exploration has attracted venture money and government attention. Helium supply has been unstable and prices volatile. Vision-language models now extract tables from old scans cheaply, and state surveys are increasingly open to releasing data.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of 15-50k USD per year per company for a basin or state atlas, area-of-interest packs of 5-25k USD, custom data services, and, later, small overriding royalties or success fees on leases won using the data.
non_obvious_insight: The value of data flips when the target commodity changes. A well that reported 'gas contains 40% hydrogen' in 1935 was a dud then, and it is a discovery lead today. Every incumbent data vendor is organized around the old commodity, so nobody re-reads the archive for byproducts. The archives are public and low-margin for the state agencies that hold them, so the moat is the extraction pipeline, cleaning and geological calibration, not data access.
first_30_days: Pick one state survey with well-documented public scans and gas-analysis reports and one target commodity (helium or hydrogen shows are the easiest to demo). Build a proof-of-concept map for one basin using a few thousand well records. Cold-email about 30 junior exploration companies and geothermal developers with the map and one concrete lead they can check. Sell 3-5 area-of-interest packs at around 5k USD each, and ask for pre-payment for the next state.

title: Real-Time Dental Benefits Texting Before December 31
one_liner: A dental-office tool that texts patients their actual remaining insurance dollars and a wallet card, filling the Q4 schedule that insurers' broken apps leave empty.
customer: Independent dental practices with 1-5 dentists, first those on Open Dental (open API) or Dentrix. The owner-dentist or office manager pays.
problem: Patients cannot find what benefit they have left. The insurers' own apps are among the worst-rated apps in the category. The Delta Dental Mobile App averages 1.49 stars over 1,809 ratings and United Concordia averages 2.48. Reviews describe 40+ login failures and complaints such as 'Doesn't let you see your EOB', 'Doesn't even show claims payments', 'App displays the wrong Member ID number' and 'Claims on app don't match claims on web'. Most benefit years reset on December 31, so treatment plans go unscheduled while the practice's front desk spends hours on the phone. Practice campaigns rely on benefit data stored in the practice software, which goes stale.
solution: Each night the tool runs real-time eligibility checks (X12 270/271 through an existing dental clearinghouse) for patients with accepted but unscheduled treatment. It calculates remaining annual maximum and deductible met. It then sends a personalized text with the patient's actual figure and a booking link, for example: 'You have $1,120 of your Delta Dental benefit left, and it expires Dec 31.' It also issues an Apple or Google Wallet pass with the insurance card and remaining balance. The front desk gets a ranked call list with expected production. There is no generative AI involved, and it works from live payer data, not from what the practice software last stored.
why_now: Today is Sept 28, 2026, so the Q4 use-it-or-lose-it window is open now and a pilot can run Oct 15 to Dec 20. Insurer apps still bounce users to a web browser to log in and show little data. Practice-software APIs and clearinghouse eligibility APIs are available to small vendors. A tool that ships in October can be measured in booked production before year end.
revenue_model: A free Q4 pilot with a 5% success fee on collected production from attributed appointments. After the pilot, $299/month flat per practice, or $199/month plus 3% of attributed production. Later add-ons: a January 'new benefits' campaign and a mid-year campaign for plans with fiscal-year resets.
non_obvious_insight: The insight is that the insurer's app is so bad that the dental office is the only interface patients trust, and the office has never been given real-time dollar figures in one place. The evidence is patient-side, not practice-side, so the practice-side demand (fuller Q4 schedules) still needs to be proven in the pilot. Evidence: Delta Dental Mobile App (1.49 stars, 1,809 ratings; 'Doesn't let you see your EOB'; login failures) at https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1585628503 and its review feed at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=1585628503/sortby=mostrecent/xml. United Concordia Dental (2.48 stars; 'Doesn't recognize my member id'; EOB PDFs fail to load; no Apple Wallet ID) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=522392221/sortby=mostrecent/xml. Practice-side friction: Dentrix reviewers cite 20+ hours on phone support during a forced migration at https://www.softwareadvice.com/dental/dentrix-profile/reviews/. The wedge sits beside the practice-management system, so the practice does not have to replace it.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: integrate the Open Dental API and one clearinghouse's eligibility API, and run the calculation on a test practice. Days 10-20: recruit 5 practices through Open Dental user forums and dentist Facebook groups, offering a free pilot with success-fee terms. Days 20-30: launch the first campaigns, tracking texts sent, appointments booked and production. Turn the results into a case study to sell more practices before mid-November and for next year's Q4.

title: CRA Ten-Year Update Vault for Vendors
one_liner: An escrow-plus-hosting service that keeps a small vendor's signed security updates, vulnerability intake and orphaned open-source dependencies alive for the EU Cyber Resilience Act's ten-year obligation if the vendor folds or an upstream dies.
customer: Small EU-selling firmware, IoT and software vendors (1-50 staff) with no security team, and the enterprise buyers and OEMs who will demand proof of continuity before they buy from them.
problem: CRA reporting duties started 2026-09-11 and the main obligations bite 2027-12-11, with no size exemption. A solo German software founder on HN (Sept 1, 2026) calls the requirement that security updates stay available for ten years, or the support period if longer, a critical burden, and notes reporting duties continue after support ends. Harmonised standards aren't published yet (core standards due Oct 31, 2026). Open-source upstreams also vanish: MinIO (61.3k stars) was archived on 2026-04-25 with no binaries, and 'no fork has gained traction'.
solution: Three parts. (1) Escrow: a reproducible-build environment, SBOM/VEX and split-custody signing keys held by the vault, released on contractual trigger events (insolvency, abandonment, twelve months without a patch). (2) Continuity hosting: a signed-update endpoint and advisory feed that stays online for ten years, plus a vulnerability-report intake and drafts for the EU single reporting platform. (3) Dependency lifeboat: patch backports and maintained forks of orphaned components that customers depend on (MinIO first). Vendors get a 'continuity certificate' to attach to tenders.
why_now: Reporting obligations are 17 days old as of today, standards are still being written, and small vendors are asking on HN what to do. The EU's own guidance creates open-source 'stewards' who face obligations but are exempt from fines, while manufacturers carry the burden, so the market will look for a commercial steward.
revenue_model: Annual escrow and hosting fee per product (EUR 1.5k-6k), a per-release fee, trigger-event activation fee, and dependency-lifeboat support contracts priced per node.
non_obvious_insight: The CRA turns 'what if you disappear?' from a founder worry into a legal duty, and escrow-style insurance sells to both the vendor and the buyer who fears the vendor's death; the compliance-tooling crowd (scanners, SBOM dashboards) does not cover it. Evidence: Ask HN by a one-person vendor on the ten-year update rule, harmonised standards timing and no size exemption (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/49520688). The EU says stewards are not subject to administrative fines (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-open-source), with the 11 Sept 2026 and 11 Dec 2027 dates at https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act. Linux Foundation research finds most open-source respondents unfamiliar with the CRA and its deadlines (https://linuxfoundation.org/research/cra-readiness). Greg Kroah-Hartman's explainer says the burden lands on commercial manufacturers (https://www.theregister.com/2025/09/30/cyber_reiliance_act_opinion_column/). Upstream death example: https://github.com/minio/minio.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: write the escrow and trigger-event contract template with an EU tech lawyer, and prototype a reproducible-build capture for one embedded Linux and one Go or Rust project. Days 10-30: post a plain-English 'CRA ten-year problem' guide on HN, the Open Regulatory Compliance working group hub and embedded-vendor communities, and offer 10 founders a free continuity assessment. Sell 3 paid pilot vaults at a founder price of EUR 1k a year. In parallel, publish a MinIO advisory-and-patch feed to test paying demand for the lifeboat.

title: Notarized Sky: Satellite Image Authenticity Desk
one_liner: A verification desk that tells insurers, traders and newsrooms whether a 'satellite photo' is real, by corroborating it against independent archives and issuing a signed chain-of-custody attestation.
customer: Marine war-risk and political-violence underwriters and brokers in the London market, commodity and energy trading desks, and verification desks at wire services and OSINT outlets. Second wave: parametric insurers whose triggers depend on Earth-observation data, and arbitration or sanctions law firms.
problem: Generative tools can now fabricate or subtly edit overhead imagery, and viral 'satellite photos' of strikes, burning tankers or troop moves circulate in every conflict, moving prices and claims. Buyers assume satellites are physics-grade truth, but the last mile is a JPEG on social media and vendors sell pixels, not provenance. With the Strait of Hormuz reportedly closed since March 2026, war-risk claims and rumor-driven price moves are large.
solution: (1) Rapid 'witness triangulation': check the claimed place and time against open archives (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2, Landsat) and quick commercial archive pulls (optical and SAR), plus sun-angle and shadow geometry, cloud and terrain consistency, and vessel positions versus AIS and RF logs. (2) Forensics for synthetic or edited artifacts and C2PA/EXIF provenance. (3) A signed, hash-timestamped corroboration report usable in claims files and disputes. (4) For imagery buyers, verify delivered files against provider manifests.
why_now: Hormuz disruption created a wave of unverifiable incident claims. EU AI Act Article 50(2) synthetic-content marking applies from 2 Dec 2026 for systems already on the market, raising attention on provenance. Commodity EO and SAR are cheap and frequent (Planet targets up to 10 revisits a day), but no cross-vendor 'signed pixels' standard exists.
revenue_model: $2.5-8K per rapid verification report (24-hour SLA) and $8-20K per month retainers for underwriters and desks. Later, metered API access for parametric insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is not the product; corroboration is. Government-held archives cannot be retroactively edited by an attacker, and SAR sees through cloud and is not something a text-to-image model can fake convincingly. A tiny team can be an independent witness cheaply. What buyers actually pay for is a defensible attestation, a SOC report for pixels, that survives a claims dispute.
first_30_days: Publish teardowns of 3 viral fake or misattributed satellite images from 2025-26 conflicts, each with reproducible multi-source refutations. Send them to 25 marine war-risk brokers and 15 newsroom verification desks. Sell 3 rapid-verification pilots at $2.5K each and convert one underwriter to a retainer.

title: Price-Raise Autopilot for One-Person Service Firms
one_liner: Find the underpriced clients in a solo operator's own invoice history and execute personalized price increases, paid as a share of the uplift.
customer: Nonemployer and 1-5 person service businesses with 50-800 repeat clients: groomers, cleaners, landscapers, bookkeepers, tutors, therapists, detailers.
problem: Rising costs are the top financial challenge, yet most solo operators have not repriced in years because they fear churn. The industry sells lead generation, not repricing, even though a modest increase on the bottom 40% of clients often beats a 20% lift in leads.
solution: Connect Stripe, Square, QuickBooks, Jobber or booking-software history. For each client, compute the effective hourly rate after drive time, materials and discounts, and rank clients as safe-to-raise or protect. Draft one-to-one messages in the owner's voice, send by text or email, track churn and replies, and roll back individual clients if needed. The dashboard shows before-and-after profit per hour.
why_now: The Fed's 2026 survey shows 76% of international sourcers already passed costs to customers, so consumers now accept increases. Payment and booking APIs give clean multi-year history, and LLMs write natural personal notes at zero marginal cost.
revenue_model: 15-20% of first-year incremental revenue captured (no uplift, no fee), or a $49/month plan for owners who prefer flat pricing.
non_obvious_insight: The industry assumes the number-one problem, getting customers, is the one to fix. For a business of one, the fastest path to profit is charging existing customers correctly, and owners are too close to their clients to do it themselves. Outcome pricing also works because the owner sees the money.
first_30_days: Run a concierge version for 20 groomers, cleaners and landscapers found in local Facebook groups, using exports and spreadsheets. Measure revenue lift and churn below 3%. Publish two before-and-after case studies and use them to price the software.

title: Tele-Drive Home for Retirement Golf Carts
one_liner: A designated-driver and remote-driving service for owner-owned golf carts in age-restricted communities, starting with humans and automating later.
customer: Residents 75+ in golf-cart towns such as The Villages, Sun City and Del Webb communities, and their adult children. Secondary payers are HOAs and developers and restaurants near town squares.
problem: In these communities the golf cart is an 80-year-old's car, with no DMV, no Uber and no bus. Crashes and cart DUIs are a recurring local news story. Families dread taking the cart away, so there is no middle path between 'keep driving' and 'lose independence'.
solution: Phase 1 (start now): a human 'ride-home' service. A driver takes the resident's own cart home and a chase driver collects them, at $15 per ride around town squares and restaurants. Phase 2: a $39-59/month Guardian retrofit for the most common cart platforms, with geofence, speed governor, breathalyzer or quick cognitive-check lockout, crash and fall alerts, and family notification. Phase 3: a 'take me home' button that lets a remote operator drive the cart home at 5-8 mph over private cart paths.
why_now: Remote-operations stacks (cheap cameras, LTE/5G, teleop tooling) are mature at low speeds. Incumbents left a gap: Voyage held a license at The Villages but was folded into Cruise, and Carteav sells whole new autonomous carts to resorts, communities and campuses rather than upgrading the carts residents already own. Insurers and HOAs are hunting for older-driver risk reductions.
revenue_model: Per-ride fees ($10-15). Monthly Guardian subscription ($39-59). HOA or developer sponsorship and restaurant partnerships. Later, insurer discounts or revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The real competitor isn't Waymo but 'no transportation'. Making driving safer instead of ending it protects dignity, which is the emotional job families are hiring for. Low speeds on private paths are where teleoperation is technically and legally tractable today, and a human-run version proves demand and maps every route before any hardware ships.
first_30_days: Embed in one community for a month. Run Friday and Saturday evening 'ride-home' service near town squares at $15 per ride and log every route and ride. Sign 20 families onto a pilot alert package. Pitch sponsorship to local restaurants and the HOA or district. Bench-test a governor, geofence and lockout kit on two carts.

title: Smoke-and-Heat Escape Benefit for Remote Teams
one_liner: An employer-paid standby membership that, when smoke, heat-dome or evacuation triggers hit, moves remote employees within hours into pre-contracted hotel rooms with a tested desk and wifi outside the hazard zone.
customer: Heads of People or Business Continuity at remote-first companies of 150-2,000 staff (dev tools, fintech, SaaS, online education) where at least 15% of employees live in US West, Southwest, Gulf Coast or Canadian wildfire belts. They have no office to fall back on and a duty-of-care gap.
problem: When AQI hits 300, a heat dome coincides with a failed AC, or an evacuation order lands, remote employees improvise: sold-out hotels, price gouging, expense fights, lost work days. Corporate travel tools are built for planned trips, and consumer OTAs cannot guarantee inventory in an evacuation. Employers carry the productivity loss and the liability but have no product to buy.
solution: Employer buys standby access. Opted-in employees are monitored by home ZIP against public feeds (AQI forecasts, NWS extreme-heat warnings, evacuation zones, NHC cone). On a trigger the employee gets a one-tap offer: a confirmed room or extended-stay unit 100-400 miles away in a cleaner or cooler basin, at a pre-contracted rate, wifi speed-tested, pet and kid rules known, paid by virtual card. Hotels earn a small standby retainer on rooms held for trigger nights. Start with mid-tier and economy properties.
why_now: The 2026 travel market is K-shaped: mid and lower hotel tiers are pressured and booking windows shrank to about 33 days, so hoteliers will trade a discount for forward-committed revenue. Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a deadly European heatwave, making hazard seasons an HR planning assumption. Remote work is now normal enough that 'work from anywhere' relocation is a benefit line item, not an emergency.
revenue_model: $6-9 per employee per month for standby access and trigger monitoring, plus room nights at the contracted rate with about 12% platform margin. A 2,000-person employer is roughly $140-215K ARR before usage. Hotel-side retainer is funded out of the margin, not charged to hotels.
non_obvious_insight: Remote work turns evacuation from an unpredictable personal disaster into a budgetable HR benefit, because the worker's office travels with them. Smoke plumes and heat domes are regional and forecastable 24-72 hours out, so rooms can be bought as standby capacity instead of emergency spot inventory. Nobody sells this because benefits vendors do not touch hotel inventory and travel vendors do not monitor hazards.
first_30_days: Pick two hazard basins: Pacific Northwest/Northern California smoke, and Phoenix/Las Vegas heat. Handshake standby rates with 15-20 mid-tier hotels and extended-stay properties on both sides of each escape corridor. Recruit 3 remote-first startups through founder and People-ops Slack communities on a pay-per-activation pilot ($0 subscription for 60 days) with 30-50 opted-in employees each. Run it manually with a Slack bot, a spreadsheet and virtual cards. Publish a 'cost of a smoke day' calculator to generate leads.

title: Humanoid Rentals for Events and Retail
one_liner: The first profitable humanoid job is spectacle: rent Unitree-class robots plus a trained show operator to brands, malls, arenas and trade shows.
customer: Experiential-marketing agencies, retail flagships, stadium and arena marketing teams, trade-show exhibitors, casinos and theme venues. Universities renting lab time come second.
problem: Everyone else pitches humanoids as factory workers, where reliability, safety and ROI are unproven. Brands want a 'robots are here' moment now but cannot buy, program and insure a $16k robot themselves.
solution: Own 6-10 units. Sell packaged experiences (greeter, product demo, dance or boxing, photo-booth persona) with an operator, choreographer, safety marshal and event insurance. Every event doubles as a demo funnel for enterprise pilot inquiries, and later as controlled data capture.
why_now: Unitree's August 2026 IPO (about $9B) and G1 pricing near $16k make fleet capex trivial, so a robot pays back in roughly 10 event-days at $1.5-2.5k a day (my estimate). Humanoid hype is at its peak and marketing budgets are chasing it. China's robot-rental-for-events market is a proof point.
revenue_model: $2-6k a day per robot with operator, $25-60k custom activations, and sponsorship fees. Add an enterprise-pilot lead-gen fee from robot vendors later.
non_obvious_insight: Entertainment tolerates a 70% success rate and teleop, because a stumble is content. The buyer pays for attention, not productivity, so humanoid economics work here years before they work on a factory floor. Note: tariffs or restrictions on Chinese robots are a risk, so keep a non-Chinese unit option.
first_30_days: Buy 2 G1s (about $32k) and build 3 scripted 10-minute acts. Cold-pitch 40 experiential agencies, minor-league teams and mall marketing managers. Book 5 paid weekend events and film content for social proof.

title: Lot Vault: Reagent Warranty Claims and Lot Registry
one_liner: A photo-the-label app that files unclaimed reagent-guarantee refunds for labs, quietly builds the only lot-level reagent performance database, and then group-buys locked good lots for small labs.
customer: Lab managers and PIs in organoid, iPSC, primary-immune-cell and antibody-heavy labs (about $79-199/month per lab). Core facilities and departments with central purchasing pay for the site-wide tier. Later, challenger reagent vendors and distributors pay for lot-level analytics.
problem: Every experienced postdoc knows the hidden variable behind failed experiments is the reagent lot: FBS, Matrigel/BME, B27, human serum, antibodies, polymerases. A lot that passes the vendor's certificate of analysis can still kill your organoids, and nobody logs lot numbers. Vendors' satisfaction guarantees require the lot number, images and a claim inside a time window, so postdocs almost never file. Money goes unclaimed. Six labs across town hit the same bad lot and never find out. When a good lot runs out, a two-year experimental series has to be re-validated.
solution: Wedge: a phone app where the postdoc snaps the vial label and taps 'worked' or 'failed', with optional gel or blot photos. On 'failed' it drafts the vendor guarantee claim with lot, dates and images, and tracks the credit. On 'worked' it logs the lot against the user's cell type and assay. Over time this becomes a crowd-sourced registry: 'Matrigel lot X: 7 of 9 organoid labs report failure.' Phase 2: when a lot shows good in at least 5 labs, the company negotiates a vendor lot reservation and runs a pooled group buy. Small labs get a locked lot for 12-24 months without needing 100 bottles of freezer space. The company takes a 10-15% margin.
why_now: NIH funding disruption and higher reagent prices from tariffs (verify current tariff levels) make labs care about every wasted dollar in 2025-26. Vision LLMs make label OCR and claim drafting almost free. Reproducibility pressure is high and the NIH is pushing rigor. Vendors are consolidating, and challenger brands need a credible independent signal to displace incumbents.
revenue_model: Subscription per lab or per core. A 10-15% margin on group-buy locked-lot sales. Success-fee or flat fee on recovered credits. Later, paid lot-analytics dashboards for challenger vendors and distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The certificate of analysis tests the vendor's assay, not yours. The only real lot-quality signal is 'the lab down the hall using my cell type', and that signal already circulates informally by hallway lore. Nobody has digitized it because no single lab has enough data. The warranty-claim refund is the Trojan horse: it gives the user immediate ROI, so people log lot numbers without being asked, and it produces the data moat.
first_30_days: Build a no-code MVP: a forwarding inbox plus a form that pulls lot number and catalog number and drafts claim emails. Recruit 15 labs from organoid and iPSC Slack and Discord channels and postdoc association lists. Offer 3 months free plus a 'we file it for you' concierge. File the first 30 claims by hand to learn each vendor's rules. Show each lab the dollars recovered. Convert to $99/month once the first credit lands. In parallel, pick one product (for example BME or FBS) and quote a pooled lot reservation to 10 pilot labs.

title: Medicaid Work-Rule Retention Packets for Health Plans
one_liner: A pay-per-retained-member service that assembles the income-proxy, exemption and medical-frailty evidence packets Medicaid expansion enrollees need to keep coverage, sold to the health plans and clinics that lose revenue when members are dropped.
customer: Medicaid managed-care plans (especially regional and provider-sponsored plans in expansion states), FQHC networks, and hospital systems with large expansion panels. Secondary buyers: state agencies and counties that have said they will not add staff.
problem: Work requirements start January 1, 2027 in 44 states. CMS projects 2.3M people lose Medicaid in 2027, and 55% of enrollees are unaware of the rule. States are scraping existing data. Nebraska hired no new staff, and its medical-frailty code list omitted certain cancers, heart failure and HIV. North Carolina bars self-attestation and requires 3 months of records. About 25% of Dare County's expansion enrollees are self-employed. County Medicaid units have ~10% vacancy and staff with only 11-13 months' experience. A KFF-cited expert calls hours tracking 'a problem no state has solved at scale.'
solution: Consent-based enrollee flow, started via text or QR code at a clinic or from a plan's outreach. The enrollee links bank, gig-platform, payroll or 1099 data through open-banking and income-verification connectors. The system computes monthly income against the $580 threshold (80 hours x $7.25) that satisfies the rule, with seasonal averaging where the state allows. It then generates a state-formatted verification submission. In parallel it mines the plan's or clinic's claims and EHR history to match the medically frail categories and produces clinician attestation forms. It tracks the 30-day grace window and 6-month redeterminations. Volunteer-hour and school verification come from partner organizations. A human navigator queue handles exceptions.
why_now: CMS issued its interim final rule June 1, 2026 and a medical-frailty implementation deck on September 8. Nebraska (May 1) and Montana (July 1) are live, so real failure modes are visible. States may request extra information from enrollees in year one, and exemption self-attestation is allowed only once before 2028, so documentation becomes mandatory after that. The January deadline sets hard budget urgency.
revenue_model: Per-packet fee plus per-member-per-month retention fee paid by the plan or clinic. Assumption to validate: a retained expansion member is worth hundreds of dollars per month in capitation, so $30-100 per retained member is easily justified. Optional state contracts priced per verification.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is evidence for people the state cannot see in wage data (self-employed, gig, seasonal), not caseworker capacity. Health plans and clinics, not states, have both the financial incentive and the claims data to prove frailty. The federal income equivalent ($580/month) turns an impossible hours-tracking problem into a cash-flow calculation. Evidence: NC counties describe the informal-economy documentation gap, 10% vacancy, no self-attestation and 3 months of records (https://www.northcarolinahealthnews.org/2026/04/30/medicaid-work-county-challenges/). Nebraska confirmed the ~$580 income option and said it will not hire or add staff (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-closer-look-at-nebraska-the-first-state-planning-to-implement-a-medicaid-work-requirement/), and its frailty code list had gaps (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/nebraska-medicaid-work-requirements-launch-first-state/818992/). CMS projects 2.3M coverage losses in 2027 (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/cms-medicaid-work-requirements-final-rule-state-guidance/821631/). State staffing gaps: https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-cuts-work-requirements-state-staff-shortages/. Risk: 26 states are suing over the rule.
first_30_days: Offer free pilots to 1-2 FQHCs in Nebraska or Montana, where enrollees already face the requirement. Build on an open-banking connector and an income-verification API. Draft the income-proxy calculator and a frailty-evidence template from CMS's September deck. Book meetings with member-retention leads at 5 regional Medicaid plans, with a paid pilot targeted for the November-December pre-January enrollment wave. Get a HIPAA BAA and consent language in place first.

title: Enclave Escrow: Buy Data by Measured Lift
one_liner: A confidential-compute clean room where the buyer's evaluation runs on the seller's data inside an attested enclave, and the price is set by the measured lift, so neither side reveals its asset before agreeing.
customer: Quant funds, ML teams and R&D groups buying alternative or proprietary datasets, and the small data sellers (satellite counts, AIS ship data, web panels, lab datasets) who cannot afford NDAs and legal cycles. Autonomous buyer agents are the growth channel.
problem: Arrow's information paradox: you cannot value data without seeing it, but once you see it you do not need to buy it. Sellers therefore refuse trials or overprice, buyers waste budget on blind purchases, and agents purchasing autonomously cannot sign NDAs or judge value.
solution: Seller uploads an encrypted dataset. Buyer uploads a hashed evaluation harness (a backtest, a fine-tune validation run, an accuracy test). Both run inside a CPU plus GPU trusted execution environment with remote attestation. Only a signed lift score leaves the enclave, under a per-pair query budget or differential-privacy noise to stop the score being used as an extraction oracle. A pre-agreed schedule converts lift into a license price, and payment triggers automatically if the buyer opts in.
why_now: Confidential computing on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs now runs with little performance penalty and produces GPU-signed attestation reports. Cloud providers and GPU-TEE clouds sell it off the shelf. Agents with pay-per-request data endpoints are starting to buy data blind.
revenue_model: 5-10% of transaction value, compute pass-through, $5-25k per paid evaluation for funds, and a subscription for private clean rooms.
non_obvious_insight: Sell the measurement, not the data. The thing placed in escrow is an experiment both sides commit to before seeing the result, which turns the sale into outcome-linked pricing and lets tiny sellers with no legal team participate. Bounding the lift oracle (query budgets) is the hard, defensible engineering piece.
first_30_days: Sign 3 small alt-data sellers and 2 small funds or ML teams for paid pilots. Use rented confidential VMs and a manually built harness for each evaluation. Charge $5k per evaluation and deliver a signed report. Use results to write a public 'pay for lift' pricing template.

title: Disposition Authority Registry for Chosen Family
one_liner: A verified registry that lets hospitals and funeral homes instantly find out who legally controls a person's body when that person is not the state's default next of kin.
customer: Solo agers, unmarried long-term partners, LGBTQ+ elders, people estranged from family, and blended-family couples pay $59 to register. Estate-planning attorneys, senior and LGBTQ+ service organizations, and hospice or palliative social work teams are the channel and secondary payers.
problem: State statutes rank who controls disposition: spouse, adult children, parents, siblings. An unmarried partner of 30 years can be shut out by a child who hasn't spoken to the deceased in a decade. When it goes wrong, the body sits in refrigeration for days or weeks while lawyers argue, and the funeral home is stuck because releasing to the wrong person means being sued. Many states allow a written designation of an agent, but witness and notary rules differ, and the signed document is in a drawer or a safe deposit box that no one can open at 2 a.m.
solution: Attorney-reviewed, state-specific designation forms completed through a remote-notary and e-sign flow. The signed document goes into a timestamped registry, with a wallet card and a phone lock-screen QR. A 24/7 verification line and API lets hospital social workers, medical examiner offices and funeral homes ask 'is there a designated agent for this person?' The designated agent is auto-notified. The record also stores preferences (cremation or burial, preferred funeral home, link to any pre-need contract).
why_now: The US has a fast-growing population of solo agers and 'elder orphans': never-married, childless, divorced or estranged. The cohort of same-sex couples who married after 2015 is now entering the age of dying. Remote online notarization and electronic signature of estate documents are now widely accepted. Healthcare advance-directive registries exist, but almost none cover disposition.
revenue_model: $59 one-time registration plus $12/year for renewal and verification upkeep. Attorney and organization white-label at $25 per registrant. Hospice, hospital and health-system site licenses at $2,000-$5,000/year for verification access. Verification is free to funeral homes so adoption is frictionless.
non_obvious_insight: The ugliest funeral disputes are almost never about money, they're about who has the pen. Funeral homes carry all the legal risk of releasing to the wrong person, so they will champion and actively check any credible registry. Everyone built registries for the living person's medical wishes, but nobody built one for the body. That is the gap where an insider watches families fight in the arrangement office.
first_30_days: Launch in three states whose statutes expressly recognize a written designation of agent. Partner with a local LGBTQ+ senior center, an elder-orphan or solo-ager meetup, and two estate attorneys who will co-host workshops. Get ten funeral homes to sign a one-page pledge to check the registry on every first call. Sell registrations at senior-center and library workshops and via a 'chosen family' landing page. Target 150-200 registrations and use the first funeral-home lookup as the case study.

title: Screwworm-Era Rescue Transport Compliance Desk
one_liner: With screwworm confirmed in Texas, dogs leaving Texas and New Mexico need a fresh vet inspection certificate and destination permits; run the compliance desk that keeps shelter transports moving.
customer: Texas and New Mexico shelters, rescue transport organizations (ground and air), destination shelters in other states, and the funders who pay for transport.
problem: New World screwworm was first confirmed in Texas on 2026-06-03, with movement restrictions in infested zones across a growing list of counties. Reports say dogs from Texas and New Mexico now need a certificate of veterinary inspection within 72 hours of movement that attests no wounds infested with screwworm. Receiving states add entry permits and pre-travel inspections five to seven days out, shelter transports are slowing, and accredited vets are scarce for 20-100 animal loads.
solution: A transport desk with a destination-state rules engine, permit and eCVI orchestration, scheduling of mobile inspection crews (floating DVM plus techs) at pickup sites, a treatment log for authorized products, manifests, and rejection-risk alerts before a truck leaves.
why_now: Screwworm's first US detection (June 2026), FDA emergency authorizations for animal drugs (15 EUAs and 3 conditional approvals as of 2026-09-03), and state zone orders have changed movement rules mid-season. Shelters are crowded and funders are looking for what unblocks flow.
revenue_model: $15-35 per animal moved, mobile inspection crew fees, and SaaS for destination shelters. Costs often covered by transport grants.
non_obvious_insight: Rescue transport is treated as a charity logistics problem. The new binding constraints are regulatory paperwork and scarce accredited-vet hours, which is a compliance-ops business with per-animal pricing. The same rails will be reused for the next outbreak (H5N1, canine influenza, rabies rule changes).
first_30_days: Call 10 Texas shelters and transport groups. Put the top 5 destination-state rule sets into a spreadsheet. Run 2 transports with hired mobile-vet pickup inspections at $20 per animal. Approach transport-grant funders for direct payment.

title: Convert Empty Thai Hotel Floors to Monthly Stays
one_liner: Take under-filled floors of mid-tier Thai hotels on revenue share and run them as furnished 30-90 day remote-worker wings, replacing lost Chinese group demand with sticky monthly stays.
customer: Owners of 80-300 room three- and four-star hotels in Bangkok, Phuket, Pattaya and Chiang Mai whose Chinese group volume collapsed. End users are remote workers, retirees and long-stay sports or wellness visitors.
problem: Thailand's 2025 arrivals fell 7.2% and sit 17% below 2019, with Chinese arrivals down 33.5%. Insiders wait for Chinese groups to return, but Chinese outbound is shifting to independent travellers who go farther and spend less on hotels. Empty floors bleed fixed costs, while nomads on 40+ visa schemes struggle to find reliable monthly stays.
solution: We take 20-40% of rooms and add a coworking corner, bonded fast internet, laundry, community events and monthly billing. Guests pay USD 650-1,100 per month including utilities, for a 30-day minimum. We market through nomad communities and groups and help with long-stay visa paperwork. The hotel keeps F&B upside.
why_now: The China demand collapse leaves stranded capacity. Thailand's long-stay Destination Thailand Visa exists for remote workers, and 40+ countries now offer nomad visas. Nomad information is now free (Nomads.com sells lifetime membership for USD 1), so operators win on product, not discovery.
revenue_model: A 20-30% management fee on room revenue or a fixed lease spread, plus ancillary revenue from SIMs, insurance and visa-service referrals.
non_obvious_insight: Hotels are optimised for nights while nomads buy months. A floor at 90% occupancy on monthly rates beats 35% occupancy at full nightly rates, and monthly guests do not pay 22-28% OTA commission.
first_30_days: Sign 2 hotels in Bangkok or Chiang Mai on a 60-day trial of 10 rooms each. Build a one-page site and post in nomad and expat groups. Target 15 monthly bookings, and record occupancy and revenue per available room against the hotel's nightly baseline.

title: Contractor Location and Payout Attestation for Sanctions Safety
one_liner: Continuous proof that remote contractors are where they say and are paid where they claim, giving employers evidence against North Korean IT-worker sanctions exposure.
customer: Startups and mid-market engineering-heavy firms using contractors, EOR and payroll platforms, staffing firms, and cyber-insurance brokers as a channel.
problem: North Korean IT-worker schemes hit 'nearly 70' and 'over 100' US companies in cases sentenced in April and May 2026. Deepfaked interviews and rented identities pass document checks, and laptops go to US-based farms. Paying a sanctioned actor is strict liability under OFAC, so the real fear for a CFO is not a fake candidate but a sanctions violation and forfeiture.
solution: Three layers: (1) a light first-90-day attestation (IP and VPN patterns, remote-access and KVM-over-IP detection, device continuity with the interview session); (2) payout-account screening (third-party or country mismatches, many workers to one account, crypto payouts); (3) shipping-address risk scoring. Output is an evidence file counsel can hand to a regulator or insurer.
why_now: The April and May 2026 sentencings show enforcement is real. Deepfake interviews are cheap and passing. The layer above hiring (payments and audit evidence) has no product, because hiring-fraud vendors focus on faces.
revenue_model: $15-30 per contractor per month, audit packs at $2-10K, insurer and broker referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The budget belongs to finance and legal, not HR or security, and the deliverable is evidence for regulators, not a risk score. Payout accounts are the chokepoint and are far easier to screen than faces.
first_30_days: Offer 20 startups a free payout-and-shipping exposure audit from a CSV export via VC platform teams and fractional-CFO networks. Convert to $500/month monitoring and sign one cyber-insurance broker.

title: Dark-Core Muscle Clinics in Converting Offices
one_liner: A plug-in metabolic and muscle clinic sized for the windowless middle of deep office floor plates that developers cannot turn into apartments, so dead space earns rent and GLP-1 users get an in-building place to keep their muscle.
customer: Office-to-residential developers and their lenders with deep-floorplate buildings (they gain a rent line on unusable area). Demand side: GLP-1 users who live or work in the building, plus employers that dropped GLP-1 coverage (employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% in 2026) and want a capped-cost program.
problem: Conversions only pencil when every bedroom can have a window, so deep floor plates lose a large share of each floor to unrentable middle or need expensive light wells. Meanwhile only about a third of non-diabetic GLP-1 patients persist at 1 year, stoppers regain weight roughly 4x faster than behavioral losers, and muscle loss is unmanaged. Nobody is paid to run a supervised strength-and-nutrition protocol close to where patients live and work.
solution: A standardized 3,000-6,000 sf module: body-composition scan, 6-8 supervised strength stations, dietitian rooms, lab draw, telehealth booths and pill-pickup lockers, run by a prescriber-agnostic clinical group so members can bring a Wegovy or Foundayo script from anywhere. Ambulatory clinics are Group B occupancy like offices, so no change of use is needed. Developers get a 'core-fill' master lease (low $/sf plus a slice of membership revenue) that improves conversion math and gives lenders a credit-tested income line. Members pay about $99/mo. Employers pay a capped per-employee fee.
why_now: The Wegovy pill (Jan 2026) and Lilly's Foundayo (Apr 2026) at about $149/mo turned GLP-1s into a mass cash-pay product, so millions of stop-and-restart cycles are coming. Employers are dropping coverage. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $289B of office loans maturing by 2028 and CMBS delinquency at 13.2%, so owners will trade rent for feasibility. Neko Health's $700M raise for a NYC launch shows urban demand for preventive scanning, yet nobody runs the muscle-and-adherence loop after the scan.
revenue_model: Memberships at $79-149/mo; per-member fees from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; body-comp and lab add-ons; a low-rent master lease with revenue share to the landlord.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that kills conversions (no daylight) is the one thing a clinic does not need. Because clinics share office occupancy class, the space is code-legal without a change of use. A clinic inside the building where hundreds of residents and lunch-hour office workers already are may be the highest-adherence location possible for a persistence problem.
first_30_days: Lease one vacant interior suite in a half-empty Class B office at near-zero rent with landlord-funded build-out. Open a 10-week 'GLP-1 muscle lab' with one exercise physiologist, a $10-15K body-composition scanner and a contracted dietitian. Sell 40-60 memberships to workers in the building and 2-3 local employers that dropped coverage. Take the adherence data to conversion developers with deep-plate buildings and sign 1-2 letters of intent.

title: Scrap-to-Tab: Supply-House Credit for Trade Scrap
one_liner: A weekly scrap-and-refrigerant buy-back inside independent HVAC, plumbing and electrical supply houses that pays contractors in credit against their supply-house tab.
customer: Independent supply houses (channel, and they benefit from lower receivables) and their solo-to-10-tech contractor accounts. Downstream buyers are scrap mills, refrigerant reclaimers and rare-earth/copper processors.
problem: Small trades are cash-starved: 1 in 5 subs waits 60+ days to be paid, and residential HVAC shipments fell 25-50% in 2025 with equipment prices about 40% above 2020. Techs burn hours hauling old coils and copper to yards, or leave value in the dumpster. Supply houses carry the credit risk on 30-60 day terms.
solution: At the counter: sorted bins, a certified scale and basic grading. Contractors drop copper, brass, aluminum coil, old compressors/motors and recovered refrigerant (handled via a licensed reclaimer). Credit posts to their account, or cash is paid minus a small fee. We settle with the supply house in cash monthly, which cuts its receivables, and sell graded loads. Later add a bounty for magnet-bearing inverter compressors and motors, sold to rare-earth recyclers.
why_now: The HFC phase-down keeps cutting virgin refrigerant, making recovered gas strategic. The Aug 2026 BIS rule shows scrap is now a national-security asset and 'may add materials'. Hyperscalers are pulling rare earths out of waste streams. The HVAC trough is squeezing small-shop cash.
revenue_model: 10-20% spread on scrap; per-pound fee on refrigerant; supply-house sponsorship; rare-earth magnet bounty.
non_obvious_insight: The supply counter is the only place every small trade shows up weekly, it already extends credit, and it is a natural sorting checkpoint. Scrap value paid as tab credit is working capital the supply house wants (lower receivables) and contractors value more than yard cash.
first_30_days: Sign two independent supply houses in one metro. Place a scale and six bins. Buy at about 85% of local yard price for 30 days, then sell to a yard and a reclaimer. Measure pounds per week and receivables reduction, and pitch other houses on days-sales-outstanding improvement.

title: Verified-Human Capture for Robot Training Data
one_liner: A trusted-capture layer that proves robot training video was really filmed by a real human doing a real task on a real sensor, sold to data vendors and to the labs that buy from them.
customer: Robot-data collection networks (the long tail beneath XDOF and Mecka) and the humanoid makers and robot-foundation-model labs that buy their hours of first-person footage.
problem: Physical-world data is the humanoid bottleneck, and vendors pay gig workers to film themselves making coffee or fixing cars. Pay-per-effort markets get swamped by slop: cURL killed its bug bounty in Jan 2026 over AI-generated reports. AI video makes fake demos trivial. Workers can replay clips, script them or run multiple accounts, and buyers cannot QC hours at scale. One contaminated batch can poison a training run. Vendors grading their own data is the referee-grading-itself problem.
solution: A capture app and a certified head- or chest-mount kit that signs raw video, IMU and depth with device-bound keys in a C2PA-compatible manifest. Physics-consistency checks compare video-derived camera motion to the IMU trace, which generated video fails. Unique-worker checks without stored biometrics (on-device liveness, payout-account binding). Random human audit sampling and per-clip QA scores. A batch-level 'Certified Real' certificate buyers can verify.
why_now: Mecka is near a $500M valuation and XDOF hit about $50M annualized revenue within three months of leaving stealth. C2PA hit critical mass (TikTok joined in Jul 2026). EU AI Act Article 50 has applied since Aug 2, 2026. Biometric proof-of-personhood is being banned in places (Thailand, Kenya, Philippines), and verifier breaches (Persona, IDScan) push toward on-device proof.
revenue_model: $0.30-$1.50 per verified hour, paid by vendors who pass it through. $20/mo certified-kit rental per collector. Enterprise audits for large data buyers, $5k-$25k per batch program.
non_obvious_insight: In content, human-made is a nicety. In robot data, physically real and human-performed is the entire product, and synthetic data is a far cheaper competitor. A certificate showing which hours are real is what lets vendors keep a price premium, so vendors will pay for it. The verifier gets a toll on the fastest-growing data category without competing with anyone.
first_30_days: Ship an open-source signed-capture app and a physics-consistency checker. Offer 5 small data vendors a free audit of one sample batch and show them the share of clips that fail. Convert 2 to paid pilots at $2k-$5k/mo. Ship a 'Certified Real' batch stamp and a public verification page.

title: Contingency Subrogation Forensics for Robot Accidents
one_liner: CCC-for-robots: a forensic recovery shop that turns warehouse-robot, AV and drone logs into fault-apportioned recovery demands for the insurers who already paid the claim.
customer: Subrogation units and TPAs at mid-size commercial P&C carriers, warehouse-focused MGAs, and brokers serving 3PLs and logistics parks.
problem: Robots damage racking, inventory, vehicles and people, and the insurer pays first, often under a policy never rated for robots. Recovery depends on whether the hardware, the model, the integrator's configuration, the operator's procedure or maintenance failed. The evidence sits in vendor-controlled logs and cloud consoles that get purged, and vendor contracts cap liability and force arbitration. Adjusters do not know what to ask for or how fast.
solution: A standard 72-hour evidence-preservation and vendor data-request package. Log parsers for the export formats of 3-5 common AMR, AGV, forklift and robotaxi platforms. A reconstruction timeline. A fault-apportionment matrix (OEM, integrator, operator, maintainer, site) with contract-cap analysis, plus a demand package addressed to the vendor's insurer.
why_now: Warehouse robot fleets, many of them imported, are scaling faster than underwriters' understanding, and trade press says insurers are unprepared. Robotaxi fleets are expanding across US cities in 2026. Carriers adding AI exclusions to GL, E&O and EPLI make 'which policy pays' a live dispute, which raises the value of recovering the loss from someone else. Claims from 2024-25 deployments are now maturing into subrogation files.
revenue_model: $3-8k flat fee per file plus 15-25% contingency on recoveries above a threshold. Later, annual retainers with carriers and a licensed evidence-request tool for adjusters.
non_obvious_insight: The first real price of AI and robot liability will be set in recovery negotiations, not in underwriting. Whoever standardises how blame is split between OEM, integrator and operator, and holds the resulting loss-cost data, becomes the rating bureau, as CCC and Verisk did in auto. The bottleneck is evidence access and speed, not legal theory.
first_30_days: Email 30 subrogation managers and TPAs offering a free reconstruction and recovery memo on one closed robot or AV claim within 10 days. Bring on an ex-robotics field-service engineer and subrogation counsel on a retainer. Write the preservation-letter pack. Aim for 2 paid files by day 60.

title: Canary Errors: Measure If Human Reviewers Still Catch Mistakes
one_liner: Phishing-simulation for 'human in the loop': plant known, harmless defects in AI drafts headed to human reviewers and sell the measured catch-rate as audit-grade proof of oversight.
customer: Risk, compliance, and legal-ops heads at 20-500 lawyer firms, medical-coding/RCM companies, claims-review shops, and AML/KYC alert-review BPOs. The malpractice and E&O carriers and brokers that cover them are the second payer and the distribution channel.
problem: Every AI risk policy ends with 'a human reviews it.' Nobody measures whether that human still catches errors. Automation bias means that as the AI gets 98% right, reviewers drift into rubber-stamping. Clients, insurers and regulators now ask for evidence of effective oversight. Lawyers have been sanctioned in hundreds of cases for fabricated AI citations, and Deloitte Australia refunded part of a government fee in 2025 over AI-hallucinated errors in a report. Firms can show that a review step exists but cannot show that it works.
solution: A thin layer between the AI draft and the reviewer: a Word/DMS plugin or queue middleware. It seeds a small percentage of items with synthetic, known-answer defects: swapped case citations, transposed numbers, altered party names, wrong ICD or CPT codes. Nothing seeded ever ships, because a defect the reviewer misses is caught by the system before release, and the reviewer gets an instant 'gotcha' micro-lesson. It records catch, miss and time per reviewer and per workflow, adapts difficulty, and outputs an 'Oversight Effectiveness Report' mapped to EU AI Act human-oversight duties, ISO 42001, SR 11-7 and client outside-counsel guidelines. The end state is a vigilance score that insurers can price against.
why_now: Agentic workflows in 2025-26 push more volume through single-click 'approve' steps. Courts and clients now punish unreviewed AI output. EU AI Act human-oversight obligations for high-risk systems are coming, even with the timeline under revision. Insurers launching AI-specific coverage (Lloyd's-backed products, AI-underwriting startups) have no data on whether human controls actually work.
revenue_model: Per-reviewer seat at $30-90/month; workflow-level enterprise licenses at $20-100k/yr; insurer-branded 'verified oversight' certificates. Later, a data partnership with carriers that gives premium credits for high catch-rates.
non_obvious_insight: The market treats human review as a binary control ('there is a human'), but it is a decaying skill: the better the AI, the worse the human vigilance, as with airline autopilot. Whoever owns the catch-rate dataset becomes the credit bureau of human oversight, and insurers will price off it. It is also a wedge into every regulated workflow, because seeding defects needs no access to the underlying model.
first_30_days: Build a .docx defect injector for contract and brief review (citation swaps, number transpositions, defined-term drift). Recruit 3 small firms or legal-ops teams and one legal-malpractice broker as design partners. Run a free two-week baseline audit on about 10 lawyers and publish an anonymized benchmark ('the average associate catches X% of seeded citation errors') for PR and inbound. Convert to $2-5k paid pilots.

title: Demumu With a Body: Paid Welfare-Check Responders
one_liner: Parent-paid check-in safety for Chinese-, Indian- and Korean-speaking students and migrants living alone abroad, where a missed check-in triggers a paid local door-knock instead of an email to someone 10,000 km away.
customer: Parents (in China, India, Korea) of students and young professionals living alone abroad, who pay about $6/month plus about $45 per dispatched welfare check. Universities' international offices are a secondary channel.
problem: The viral Chinese app 'Are You Dead?' (renamed Demumu) proves demand for solo-living safety, but its only action is an email alert to two emergency contacts. For migrants those contacts are usually parents or friends in another city or country who cannot physically check. China has more than 125 million one-person households, projected at 200 million by 2030. About two-thirds of solo dwellers are aged 20-59, i.e. young migrants rather than the elderly.
solution: A student-controlled check-in app (student chooses the circle, parents pay). After a missed check-in, the escalation is: push, SMS and call, then roommates and landlord, and finally a vetted local responder who does a door-knock with a photo-verified report and can escalate to the local non-emergency welfare-check line or emergency services. The responders are recruited from the same student and gig pool as China's 'companion economy' providers, in host cities such as Boston, London, Sydney and Toronto.
why_now: Demumu's rebrand and global launch in January 2026 put the format on top of app charts in China and among paid utilities in the West, so users now trust the idea. Anyone can clone the basic check-in app in a weekend, since it reportedly cost about ¥1,500 to build. The defensible layer is physical response, which the viral app doesn't have. A 50 billion yuan ($7.4B) Chinese 'companionship economy' shows that people pay for on-demand human presence.
revenue_model: $6/month parent subscription, plus $45 per dispatch or prepaid packs of two. Later, university international-office licensing and insurer partnerships (travel and student health plans).
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the solo-liver. It is the anxious relative paying $30-60k a year in tuition, for whom $6/month is trivial. The viral product's critical gap is what happens after the alert. Evidence: Demumu reportedly cost about ¥1,500 ($210) to build, alerts two emergency contacts by email, most solo dwellers are 20-59, and there are 125 million one-person households (https://theconversation.com/are-you-dead-chinas-viral-app-reveals-a-complex-reality-of-solo-living-and-changing-social-ties-274536). It was the top paid app in China at 8 yuan and hit the top paid utilities in Australia (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/14/chinese-app-are-you-dead-to-change-name-after-surge-in-popularity and https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-15/are-you-dead-app-changes-name-demumu/106228484). Companion providers already earn 3,000-5,000 yuan/month and one hiking firm grew from under 10 to 370 workers (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/hiking-hotpot-lonely-consumers-china-031456787.html), so a responder supply pool exists.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: White-label a check-in flow (Twilio plus a simple app or LINE/WeChat mini-program) and write parent-facing Chinese copy. Recruit and vet 10 responders (graduate students) in 3 cities, with a code of conduct and background check. Days 8-20: Post on Xiaohongshu 'studying abroad' and 'parents of overseas students' and in WeChat parent groups, offering a free first month. Days 21-30: Convert 100 parent subscribers, run at least 3 real dispatches and publish the anonymized outcomes. Test privacy and consent wording with 20 students, because the student must opt in and control the circle. Assumption to test: parents' willingness to pay, and student acceptance.

title: Sunset Software Co: Pledge-Funded Tool Revival
one_liner: When a B2B tool announces its shutdown, customers pre-commit to paid 'extended life' contracts, and a small operator takes over only if a threshold is met.
customer: Companies stranded when a small dev or data tool shuts down or is acqui-hired away: CI runners, SQL clients, project trackers, metrics services. The founder of the dying tool is the second counterparty and receives a revenue share.
problem: Acqui-hires and product-gap closures strand paying customers with 30-90 days notice. BuildJet closed runners on 31 Mar 2026 because 'GitHub has made substantial improvements.' Cirrus CI closed on 1 Jun 2026 when Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI. Garnix shut down after being acquired. One customer wrote 'I have two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter.' Founders cannot sell the code. An Ask HN founder 'couldn't sell the codebase', and a commenter said 'no one wants some abandoned open source project for a defunct business.' PopSQL, SeekWell and Pivotal Tracker left solo builders racing to fill the gap.
solution: Run a 'continuity pledge' during the notice window. The customer signs a 12-month extended-life contract at 1.2-1.5x the old price, conditional on the operator reaching a minimum pledge total, like a Kickstarter for revival. If the threshold is met, the operator takes a code and brand licence, keeps the service running with a founder retainer or revenue share, and gets paid from day one. If not, nobody pays and nothing is bought. Portfolio economics do the rest: many small tools, shared infrastructure, no CAC.
why_now: AI-lab and platform acqui-hires now regularly turn small devtools into shutdown notices. Cirrus Labs joined OpenAI, Bun joined Anthropic, Astro joined Cloudflare, and Tailwind joined Shopify in the last year. The acquirer wants the team, not the customers. Permissive licences (Cirrus relicensed Tart and related tools as 'more permissive') make forks legal. The SimpleClosure H1 2026 report shows shutdowns running at scale.
revenue_model: 60-80% of extended-life fees kept by the operator, with 20-40% shared with the founder for 12 months. Later, cross-sell hosted plans to the open-source user base.
non_obvious_insight: A dying tool's code has no buyers, but its running service has customers who will pay. The sellable asset is customer continuity, and the pledge threshold removes the risk of buying dead code. Evidence: the Ask HN thread has a founder who could not sell his codebase and a commenter saying no one wants an abandoned project (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44398065). Cirrus CI's closure and Tart relicensing are covered at https://cirruslabs.org/ (HN discussion 47730194, 282 points). The Garnix thread has the 'two CI providers to replace by the end of the Quarter' comment (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48317043). BuildJet's notice sets the 31 Mar 2026 date (https://buildjet.com/for-github-actions/blog/we-are-shutting-down). Demand for a replacement shows up as solo builders rushing in, for example Saturn SQL after PopSQL and SeekWell (https://saturnsql.com) and the 10 teams racing to replace Pivotal Tracker (https://bye-tracker.net).
first_30_days: Week 1: set up a monitor on HN, status pages and changelogs for shutdown announcements. Week 2: pick one tool currently in its notice window and email the founder with a 12-month revenue-share offer. Weeks 3-4: publish a pledge page for that tool with a fixed pledge threshold and a 21-day deadline. If it clears the threshold, sign the licence and run the tool on shared infrastructure.

title: Lien-Release Chasing for Title Agents
one_liner: A per-release service that finds who now owns an old paid-off mortgage, sends the statutory demand, and chases the lender by voice, email and mail until the release is recorded.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and attorney closing offices, plus underwriters' curative departments. Priced per release delivered.
problem: An ALTA survey of 449 title professionals in 47 states (March 2026) found 59% name securing releases for prior mortgages as the most significant curative challenge. 60% of purchases need 3-5 title issues cleared before closing, over 90% involve mortgage payoffs, and 80%+ require reviewing at least 11 documents. HousingWire (September 25, 2026) reports search and exam is still mostly manual and files stall most on older or rural county records. A DataTrace study found generic public-record AI missed meaningful title matters in 40.8% of 200 searchable files, though that is a vendor study.
solution: Given a commitment with open-of-record mortgages, the system identifies the current holder or servicer from the chain of assignments, MERS servicer data and bank merger histories. It finds the right release department or statutory agent and sends a compliant satisfaction demand for that state. Voice agents work lender IVRs and phone queues, with email and certified-mail follow-up on a schedule. It monitors county recorder indexes and e-recording confirmations, uses lost-satisfaction affidavit routes where allowed, and posts a clear event back to the agent's title software. Human curative specialists take escalations such as executive letters to banks.
why_now: Title premiums hit $4.5B in Q1 2026 and volume rose nearly 14% in 2025, while ALTA says title costs fell about 5% even as operational demands and fraud work grew. Search-and-exam automation is crowded and improving (Qualia and others), which pushes the human bottleneck to the curative chase. Voice agents can now handle multi-turn calls with lender phone trees.
revenue_model: Fee per release delivered ($75-250 to test), success-only, plus a monthly minimum for agencies with steady volume. Upsell to underwriters as a curative-outsourcing vendor.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is automating search and exam, but the survey says the hardest part is the human chase for releases, which is phone- and letter-heavy, statute-driven and rules-based, and has no dominant product. Most states set deadlines and penalties for lenders that fail to record satisfactions, so a correctly formatted demand gets a response (statute detail is my domain knowledge and needs verifying by state). Evidence: ALTA study (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/alta-study-title-production-complexity-curative-work/), the manual search-and-exam story (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/title-search-exam-manual/), and the AI-miss study (https://www.housingwire.com/articles/public-record-linked-ai-misses-key-title-issues-in-many-searches/).
first_30_days: Sign 3 title agencies as design partners with their first 20 releases free. Have them share historic release requests to seed a database of the top 200 servicers and bank-merger successors. Build demand templates for the 10 highest-volume states and a voice agent for the top lenders' release lines. Start charging per release by day 30 and log turnaround days versus the agency's manual baseline.

title: Outpatient Parvo Kits for Shelters and Low-Cost Clinics
one_liner: Parvo is treated as inpatient-only, but a standardized ambulatory protocol in a box plus remote nurse monitoring can cut cost per case dramatically for shelters that otherwise euthanize.
customer: Municipal animal services, shelters and spay-neuter/low-cost clinics. Secondary: urgent-care clinics serving low-income clients.
problem: Inpatient parvo care often costs thousands of dollars, so shelters and owners choose euthanasia, and vets suffer moral distress. The briefing notes vet care is nearly half of pet-cost inflation since 2019 and that clinicians routinely alter plans for money. The outpatient protocols exist (Colorado State published one in 2017 reporting survival in the range of hospitalization; re-verify in the pilot) but only as PDFs, not as a product with logistics.
solution: A vet-signed kit per case (SC fluids, maropitant, antibiotics, syringes, nutrition support, dosing cards, video training) sold by a partner clinic-of-record. Twice-daily photo/video/weight/hydration logs are reviewed by an RVT desk with DVM sign-off, with hard escalation rules to inpatient transfer. A shared outcome registry proves results to funders. Extend to other ambulatory-able acute problems (uncomplicated gastroenteritis, SC-fluid CKD cats).
why_now: Access philanthropy just scaled (Duffield 2026-09-17; PetSmart Charities), and funders want cost-per-outcome evidence. Shelters are overcrowded and Texas transports have been slowed by screwworm restrictions. Remote VCPR rules are loosening piecemeal, and spectrum-of-care thinking is now mainstream.
revenue_model: $150-300 per case for kit plus monitoring, versus thousands for inpatient care. Annual shelter subscription ($2-5K) with usage tiers, often paid from grant dollars. Protocol licensing to low-cost clinic chains.
non_obvious_insight: The 'standard of care' for parvo is partly a business-model artifact: hospitals are paid to hospitalize. Nobody sells the cheaper protocol as a logistics-and-monitoring product, and the buyers (shelters, funders) are motivated by lives saved per dollar.
first_30_days: Partner with 3 shelters and one shelter-medicine vet. Assemble kits from wholesale distributors via the vet's prescriptions. Run 20 cases with structured data on survival, days to eating and cost. Apply for a $10K micro-grant to underwrite the pilot. Publish a one-page outcomes summary.
